title: How to keep your training video library up to date with your product
summary: How to audit and refresh your training video library after product changes, UI updates, or rebrands, without rebuilding from scratch.
body_markdown:
A customer education team on one of our calls this year had a library of more than 980 videos. Their question was what to do with the ones that already exist, which are "quickly going out of date." Making videos wasn't their problem. Keeping 980 of them true while the product kept shipping underneath was.


**The short answer:** after every release, list what changed in the product, map each change to the screens it touched, and search your library for the videos that show those screens. Fix first the videos that would stop a viewer from finishing the task, then re-record in batches grouped by screen rather than by video. Give every video a named owner so the next release gets the same check.


## Why do training videos go out of date so fast?


Training video maintenance is the work of keeping a library of recorded walkthroughs accurate as the product they show keeps changing. A video goes stale when a viewer following it sees a different screen, label, or sequence from the one on their own monitor, which makes the instruction wrong rather than merely old.


Rename a button and a help article needs one edited sentence. A video carries that button in the frame, the narration, the captions, and the cursor path, and every translated version carries it again. Teamworks met this in its first week: the education lead launched the company's first academy, and a week later he was told the whole course had to be redone.


You can size your own exposure in a few minutes. Count the releases your product team shipped last quarter, then count the videos that show navigation, settings, or the home screen, since those are the screens most releases touch. Multiply the two and you have the number of release-and-video pairs someone should have checked. Compare it with the number of checks that actually happened.


## How do you find which videos went out of date after a release?


Start from the release, not from the library. The median video exported from Clueso runs 118 seconds, so watching 200 of them end to end takes about 6.5 hours before anyone fixes anything. A list of changes narrows that to the handful of videos a release actually touched.


1. **List what changed, from two sources.** Pull the release notes, then walk the areas they mention in a test account. Release notes skip small changes. One team described a new text field that appeared in their product overnight and never made the notes, because it was too small a change to announce.
2. **Turn each change into search terms.** Write down the old label, the new label, and the screen it lives on. "Settings moved from the sidebar to the profile menu" gives you three terms to search for: Settings, sidebar, and the name of the page.
3. **Search transcripts and captions for the old terms.** Transcripts let you check a whole library for a term in seconds. Treat a match as a reason to review, since a label can appear in a sentence that is still true.
4. **Check the frames for what the narration never says.** Narrators rarely name the button they click. Scrub each flagged video at the moments the changed screen appears, and check thumbnails and title cards for old names.
5. **Record a verdict against each flagged video.** Use three states: blocks the task, misleads but the task still works, or cosmetic. Those states feed the triage in the next section.


Three situations change the steps:


- **If the release was a rebrand,** your change list is the old logo, colors, and product names rather than workflows. Our guide to[finding old brand assets after a rebrand](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-find-and-replace-old-brand-assets-after-a-rebrand) covers that search.
- **If you can't tell which screens a video shows without watching it,** start a screen map now. Another team on our calls put the goal as maintaining "a catalog of what screen appears in which video." The cheapest moment to add a video to that catalog is the day you publish it.
- **If the same screens appear in written help,** run the same check on your articles. Our post on[updating help center articles automatically](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-automatically-update-help-center-articles) covers the documentation side.


Retiring a video is a legitimate fix, and usually the fastest one in the table. For the mechanics of changing one part of a single video, see our upcoming guide to updating part of a training video without re-recording the whole thing.


Give priority to anything embedded where a viewer can't easily look elsewhere: an onboarding flow, an in-app help panel, or a required LMS course. In a required course the viewer can't skip past the wrong step, so the confusion ends up in a support ticket.

## How do you decide which outdated videos to fix first?


Ask what happens to a viewer who follows the video today, and how many viewers there are. A setup video that every new customer watches, and that now sends them to a menu that no longer exists, goes to the top of the queue. An old logo in a rarely watched video waits for the next batch.


Then pick the smallest fix that makes the video accurate again:


What changed


The smallest fix that restores accuracy


A label or term, with the screens unchanged


Edit the script and captions, then regenerate the voiceover


One screen or step inside a workflow that still works


Re-record that segment only


The order of steps, or what the task produces


Re-record the workflow and rewrite the script from the new recording


The feature is gone, or a newer video covers it


Retire the video and point its links at the replacement

## How do teams re-record training videos at scale?


Group the work by the screen that changed. If a redesigned settings page touches 14 videos, record the new settings page once, in one session and one test account, and use that footage in all 14. Fixing the same 14 videos one at a time means setting up the account, the demo data, and the recording 14 times.


1. **Group flagged videos by the screen that changed.** One redesigned page is one recording session, however many videos show it.
2. **Prepare one test account for the whole batch.** Reuse the same demo data, so a refreshed segment shows the same customer names as the footage around it.
3. **Record each changed screen once, and narrate roughly as you go.** Don't restart when you fumble a sentence, because the script gets rewritten in the next step. Our guide to[making customer training videos from product recordings](https://www.clueso.io/blog/customer-training-videos-from-product-recordings) explains why the recording should come before the script.
4. **Rewrite the script from the new recording.** Editing the old script toward the new screen is how a video ends up describing two versions of the product at once.
5. **Re-apply the same template.** Title cards, caption style, and voice settings should match the rest of the series, or the refreshed segment looks patched in.
6. **Replace the published file in place.** Swapping the file behind an existing link keeps embeds, course records, and view history intact.

## Who should own training video maintenance?


One person owns the library, and every video in it has a named owner. The library owner's job is to get the change list before the release ships, run the audit, and assign a fix type to each flagged video.


Ask product to tag any release item that changes navigation, labels, or the order of steps, and to give you a staging build. Then the audit starts before customers see the change.


Then set a service target you can actually hit, such as refreshing any onboarding video within 5 working days of a release. Track two numbers: the days between a release and its refreshed videos, and the count of videos flagged but not yet fixed. If the second number grows release after release, you need more production capacity or fewer videos, and the retire column in your triage is where to find them.


## Frequently asked questions


### How do you set a recurring refresh cadence for training videos?


Audit after every release that changes navigation, labels, or workflows, starting from the release notes. Add a quarterly sweep of the whole library for the small changes the notes missed and for videos nobody has opened since launch. Set a tighter target for onboarding and required-course videos than for long-tail tutorials.


### Which platforms update training videos automatically?


Most video tools require you to re-record and re-edit by hand. A few can re-record or regenerate a video from the current product, Clueso among them through Clueso Agents and the auto update agent add-on on its Enterprise plan. Whatever the tool, someone still has to choose which videos to refresh and review the result before it ships.


### How can you update a training video without re-recording it?


If the screens haven't changed and only a term or instruction has, edit the script and captions and regenerate the voiceover. If one step changed, re-record that segment and leave the rest of the video alone. Re-record the whole video only when the order of steps or the outcome of the task changed. Our upcoming guide to updating part of a training video covers the edit step by step.


### After a rebrand, how do you find every video that still shows the old branding?


Search transcripts and captions for old product and feature names first, since those are the fastest hits. Then check what text search can't reach: intro and outro sequences, title cards, thumbnails, and on-screen logos. Log every hit against the video in your inventory so the fixes can be batched.


## What should you do before your next release?


Before your next release ships, take your 10 most-watched videos and write down every screen each one shows. That list is the first page of your screen map. When the release notes arrive, you'll know which of those 10 videos need a look before anyone presses play.
